hints: Look closely at the two ends that will join - the -COOH on the left amino acid and the -NH2 on the right amino acid. What small molecule is always released when these two groups react?
Think about exactly which atoms leave to make that water - which part comes from the -OH of the carboxyl group and which part comes from the -H of the amino group.
Now focus on what is left behind to link the two amino acids - how does the carbon of the first join directly to the nitrogen of the second to make the -CO-NH- link?
walkthrough:
Spot the Condensation Pair**
You have two amino acids side by side. Joining them is a condensation reaction, which means you remove the elements of water and join the leftovers. The -OH comes from the carboxyl (-COOH) group of the left amino acid, and one -H comes from the amino (-NH2) group of the right amino acid.

Make the Peptide Bond**
Once that -OH and -H have left as $H_2O$, the carbon (C=O) of the first amino acid bonds directly to the nitrogen (N-H) of the second. That link, -CO-NH-, is the peptide bond. It is always C to N in that direction.

Draw the Complete Dipeptide**
Your finished drawing should show: the first amino acid intact except its -OH is gone, the second intact except one H from its amino group is gone, the new -CO-NH- bond in the middle, plus free $H_2O$ shown as a product. Keep both $R_1$, $R_2$, all other H atoms and the terminal $-NH_2$ and $-COOH$ clearly shown.

Final answer: Condensation between -COOH of first amino acid and -NH2 of second amino acid releases $H_2O$ formed from -OH + -H. Peptide bond -CO-NH- forms between C of carboxyl and N of amino: $H_2N-CH(R1)-CO-NH-CH(R2)-COOH$ + $H_2O$.

hints: Compare the two structures in Fig. 2.1 - every group is identical except for one position labelled differently. Which position is the variable part?
Think about what makes 20 different amino acids possible if they all share the same central $NH_2-CH-COOH$ backbone.
walkthrough:
The Common Backbone Plus One Variable**
Every amino acid has the same central pattern: a central carbon attached to $-NH_2$, $-COOH$, $-H$ and one extra group. That extra group is labelled R. It is sometimes called the side chain or variable group or residual group.

R Decides Identity**
There are 20 amino acids because there are 20 different possible R groups, from tiny $-H$ in glycine to larger carbon chains or rings. Because Fig. 2.1 labels them $R_1$ and $R_2$, it is telling you the two amino acids have different R groups and are therefore two different types of amino acid.
Final answer: $R_1$ and $R_2$ are the R groups / side chains / variable groups. They differ in each type of amino acid, so the two amino acids shown are different amino acids.

hints: Look at Fig. 2.2 and trace the chain shape from left to right - does it coil up or run straight? Recall the 3D shape of amylose for contrast.
Remember that amylose is made only of alpha-glucose with alpha-1,4 bonds. What does the alternating up-down orientation of the units in Fig. 2.2 tell you about the monomer type in cellulose?
walkthrough:
Chain Shape**
Fig. 2.2 shows a flat, extended ribbon with each glucose alternating orientation ($CH_2OH$ up, then down, then up). That gives a straight linear molecule. Amylose, built from alpha-glucose, has bond angles that make the chain coil into a helix, good for compact storage.

Monomer Type and Rotation**
Cellulose uses beta-glucose joined by beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, while amylose uses alpha-glucose joined by alpha-1,4 bonds. To form those beta-1,4 links, every second beta-glucose is rotated 180 degrees relative to its neighbour, which is exactly the flip-flop pattern you can see in Fig. 2.2.

Final answer: Cellulose is straight / linear, amylose is helical / coiled; cellulose is made of beta-glucose with beta-1,4 glycosidic bonds, amylose of alpha-glucose with alpha-1,4 bonds; alternate glucose residues in cellulose are rotated / inverted.

hints: Start from the shape you identified in (b) - if cellulose chains are long and straight, how might many of them pack together side by side?
Think about all those -OH groups on glucose - what type of bond can form in large numbers between neighbouring chains?
Link that packing to the job of the wall - when water enters by osmosis the cell swells, so what mechanical property must the wall provide?
A wall cannot be solid - substances still need to reach the cell surface membrane. What does a mesh of criss-cross fibres allow?
walkthrough:
From Straight Chains to Bundles**
Because each cellulose molecule is straight and linear, 60-70 molecules can lie parallel together like strands of rope. This close parallel packing is the key starting point.

Hydrogen Bonding for Strength**
Each glucose has free -OH groups sticking out sideways. Between adjacent chains these form thousands of hydrogen bonds. Individually weak, together they bundle chains into microfibrils, then into larger fibres. That cross-linked bundle has very high tensile strength.

Resisting Turgor Pressure**
When a plant cell takes up water by osmosis it becomes turgid and pushes out on the wall. The cellulose fibre network resists stretching and prevents the cell bursting, while still allowing the cell to stay firm and provide support to the plant.

Strong But Leaky**
In the wall, fibres are laid down in layers at different angles, a criss-cross arrangement that gives strength in all directions. There are many gaps between fibres, so water and solutes can pass freely through - the wall is fully permeable and does not block transport to the membrane.

Final answer: Straight chains lie parallel and form many hydrogen bonds between molecules, forming fibrils / microfibrils and fibres; gives high tensile strength to resist turgor and prevent bursting; fibres laid at angles / criss-cross in layers; gaps between fibres make wall fully permeable.
